curations.uncertainty: Acts presents a particular episode and rhetorical narrative; it does not reduce the city’s diverse population to one cult or establish every archaeological identification.
curations.why: The shared narrative directly connects Ephesus with its historical and cultic context cluster.

curations.why: The passage directly situates the Roman road-network synthesis within the Macedonia place record.

curations.uncertainty: Acts leaves Lydia’s wealth, citizenship, marital status, and formal office unspecified; Philippians 4 does not identify Euodia or Syntyche as Lydia.

curations.uncertainty: The historical synthesis includes archaeological and inscriptional evidence from different periods; it does not identify all remains with Paul’s stay.
curations.why: The passage directly joins the place record to the city-specific civic and household evidence.

curations.uncertainty: The sources do not supply a continuous itinerary or identify the couple’s Roman house archaeologically; the relation summarizes distinct episodes rather than a complete biography.
curations.why: These textual settings make Aquila’s role in the Roman household and coworker network discoverable through the Rome context record.

curations.textual_observation: Romans commends Phoebe of Cenchreae to its recipients, names her as diakonos and prostatis, and requests her welcome and assistance.
curations.uncertainty: The passage does not explicitly call Phoebe the letter carrier or interpreter; those roles are scholarly proposals, and the Greek titles have a debated semantic range.
curations.why: The Rome context gathers the textual, travel, and social questions surrounding Phoebe’s commendation to a Roman audience.

curations.textual_observation: Romans addresses its recipients as being in Rome and later names people and assemblies associated with the city; the Rome place record and contextual synthesis anchor their accounts in these passages.
curations.uncertainty: The relation concerns the city named in the letter and its textual settings; it does not identify specific houses or map every greeting to a recoverable address.
curations.why: The letter’s opening identifies Rome as the destination and grounds the local context object in its primary literary setting.

curations.original_notes: cross as sacrificial climax
curations.textual_observation: Romans 3:21-26 interprets Jesus’ death with sacrificial and redemption language, while Isaiah 53 and Hebrews 10 provide additional canonical contexts for suffering and offering.
curations.uncertainty: Paul’s hilastērion language in Romans 3:25 and Hebrews’ offering imagery admit interpretive discussion; the relation does not collapse distinct metaphors or establish a single atonement model.
curations.why: The passages make the crucifixion’s sacrificial interpretation discoverable through the Sacrifice Theme record.

curations.original_notes: deliverance meal and blood
curations.textual_observation: Exodus 12 narrates the Passover sacrifice and meal, including the blood sign; the Sacrifice Theme record includes the passage in its survey of sacrificial texts.
curations.uncertainty: The classification follows the text’s Passover-specific terminology and does not collapse later uses of sacrifice into one uniform ritual or doctrine.
curations.why: This independently authored direction connects the sacrifice theme to the Passover event through their shared textual anchor.

curations.textual_observation: The Sonship Theme includes Galatians 4, where Paul connects sonship, the Spirit, and inheritance; the kinship dossier supplies passage-specific historical controls.
curations.uncertainty: The metaphor draws on ancient kinship and inheritance concepts but does not map one-to-one onto a single Roman legal status or settle contemporary theological conclusions.
curations.why: This authored direction moves from the canonical theme to the detailed evidence and cautions for a Pauline use of sonship language.

curations.textual_observation: Exodus 14 narrates Israel’s passage through the sea and the destruction of the pursuing force; the Exodus and crossing records both anchor their account in this sequence.
curations.uncertainty: The biblical text does not securely identify the precise modern location of the sea crossing; proposed route reconstructions remain disputed.
curations.why: The chapter is the textual event at the center of the authored deliverance relationship.

curations.original_notes: life overcoming death
curations.textual_observation: Paul contrasts death through a human being with resurrection through a human being and explicitly sets Adam and Christ in parallel in 1 Corinthians 15:21-22.
curations.uncertainty: Paul names Adam and Christ but does not quote Genesis 3 in these verses; interpreters debate the precise relation of the Adam tradition to Genesis and other Jewish readings.
curations.why: The Pauline passage offers a canonical reading of human death and life in resurrection through the Adam–Christ contrast, making the Fall and Resurrection Theme records meaningfully navigable together.

curations.original_notes: Thessalonica was a major city of Roman Macedonia.
curations.textual_observation: Paul addresses the Thessalonian assembly and says their example became known in Macedonia and Achaia; the historical context connects the city with the province of Macedonia.
curations.uncertainty: First Thessalonians 1:7-8 names Macedonia and Achaia but does not itself give the city’s administrative status; Acts 17 and historical sources provide the city-specific context.
curations.why: The passage situates the Thessalonian community within a named regional network and the place record’s wider Macedonian setting.

curations.original_notes: The inscriptions and later burials are local evidence.
curations.textual_observation: Acts 17 narrates Paul’s arrival and activity in Thessalonica; the place record and historical context both use this episode alongside the Thessalonian letters.
curations.uncertainty: Acts and the letters are distinct witnesses; inscriptions and later funerary evidence contextualize the city but do not independently identify every Pauline gathering place.
curations.why: The shared narrative directly anchors the city-specific civic and funerary context to Thessalonica.

curations.original_notes: Chronology-controlled geographic, civic, Jewish-gentile, cultic, household, labor, conflict, funerary, and interpretive evidence.
curations.textual_observation: Acts 17 places Paul’s mission in Thessalonica; inscriptions and literary sources in the cluster add evidence about civic titles, households, associations, and funerary practice.
curations.uncertainty: Inscriptions and funerary evidence illuminate the city but cannot prove the identity of Paul’s hosts, synagogue location, or all participants in the assemblies.
curations.why: The authored evidence-cluster edge offers the city’s textual setting together with the contextual sources needed to interpret it.

curations.original_notes: the city itself
curations.textual_observation: First Kings 8 places the ark and the temple dedication in Jerusalem; both records use the passage to anchor the city’s significance in Israel’s worship and royal history.
curations.uncertainty: The passage’s account of divine presence and the temple is interpreted differently across later biblical texts and traditions; this link is limited to its textual setting.
curations.why: The shared chapter gives readers a direct route from the city-focused FAQ to the Jerusalem place record.

curations.original_notes: the feast itself
curations.textual_observation: Exodus 12 establishes the Passover rite and its memorial function; the FAQ and Passover event records both use that passage as a primary anchor.
curations.uncertainty: Later biblical texts reuse Passover language in distinct contexts; the connection does not imply that every later interpretation has identical meaning.
curations.why: The shared passage supplies a direct route from the explanatory FAQ to the festival event it discusses.

curations.original_notes: the risen Lord
curations.textual_observation: Paul identifies Christ as raised and names appearances to Cephas, the Twelve, and others while grounding his argument about resurrection.
curations.uncertainty: The list and order of appearances are those preserved in this Pauline passage and are not an exhaustive account of all Gospel appearances.
curations.why: This passage directly connects the FAQ’s explanation of resurrection significance with the Jesus person record.

curations.original_notes: the event itself
curations.textual_observation: First Corinthians 15 rehearses the tradition of Jesus’ death, burial, resurrection, and appearances and develops its significance for the dead.
curations.uncertainty: Paul’s argument here is not identical in form to the Gospel narratives; the relationship points to the shared resurrection claim, not to a harmonized chronology.
curations.why: The passage is a direct textual anchor shared by the FAQ and the Resurrection event record.

curations.original_notes: patriarch of promise
curations.textual_observation: Genesis 12:1-3 narrates Abram’s call and the promise that he will become a great nation and be associated with blessing among the families of the earth.
curations.uncertainty: The later canon develops Abraham’s significance in diverse ways; this link identifies the foundational narrative without settling subsequent theological interpretations.
curations.why: The shared passage directly anchors the FAQ’s introduction to the Abraham person record.

curations.original_notes: deliverer of Israel
curations.textual_observation: Hebrews 3:1-6 compares Jesus with Moses and describes Moses as a faithful servant in God’s house; both records use the passage in presenting Moses.
curations.uncertainty: Hebrews’ comparison has a distinct christological argument and should not be treated as a summary of every Hebrew Bible portrayal of Moses.
curations.why: The shared text directly links the FAQ to the person record through a New Testament interpretation of Moses.

curations.original_notes: apostle Paul
curations.textual_observation: Acts 9 narrates Saul’s encounter, blindness, and reception into the community; the FAQ and Paul person record both use this episode to anchor Paul’s biography.
curations.uncertainty: Acts and Paul’s own retrospective account in Galatians 1:11-24 differ in emphasis and detail; the relationship does not harmonize every chronology question.
curations.why: The shared passage directly connects the explanatory FAQ to the person record and the narrated conversion account.

curations.original_notes: apostle Peter
curations.textual_observation: Matthew 16 narrates Peter’s response at Caesarea Philippi and Jesus’ reply; the FAQ and Peter record both use this episode in presenting Peter.
curations.uncertainty: The saying about the “rock” and the authority language in Matthew 16 have received competing interpretations; the link does not decide among them.
curations.why: The shared passage directly grounds the FAQ’s person-level introduction in a canonical narrative about Peter.

curations.original_notes: Provides route, station, water, and identification evidence while preserving uncertainty.
curations.textual_observation: The wilderness narrative records water shortages at Marah and Rephidim; the route-and-water context gathers textual and geographic evidence for those stations.
curations.uncertainty: The exact modern locations of Marah and Rephidim are not securely established, and route reconstructions vary.
curations.why: This edge connects the broader wandering event with a focused resource and itinerary analysis.

curations.original_notes: curated canonical context
curations.textual_observation: Exodus 19 narrates Israel’s arrival at Sinai during the wilderness journey and describes Moses’ role as intermediary with the people.
curations.uncertainty: Exodus 19 is a bounded Sinai episode, not an account of the entire wilderness period or a complete itinerary.
curations.why: This passage grounds one episode of Moses’ leadership within the larger wilderness-wandering record.

curations.original_notes: curated canonical context
curations.textual_observation: Revelation 20:11-15 narrates the great white throne, judgment of the dead, and the book of life within the book’s final vision sequence.
curations.uncertainty: The imagery draws on Danielic court and apocalyptic traditions; interpretations of the judgment, books, and “second death” differ.
curations.why: The shared passage directly grounds the event record in the writing and literary structure of Revelation.

curations.original_notes: curated canonical context
curations.textual_observation: Isaiah 65 promises new heavens and earth and a renewed Jerusalem; Revelation’s New Jerusalem vision receives and transforms prophetic renewal imagery.
curations.uncertainty: Revelation 21 also draws on Ezekiel 40-48 and other texts; the relationship is a complex reception of prophetic imagery, not a one-source quotation.
curations.why: This authored link connects the writing of Revelation with one prophetic source for its city and new-creation imagery.
